definition: A connection between two vertices of a graph. In an undirected graph an edge {u, v} can be followed both ways; in a directed graph an edge (u, v) goes from u to v only. The number of edges is usually written m.
example: In a road map, each road segment between two junctions is an edge.

definition: A graph whose edges have a direction, written u→v, so you can follow them only from u to v. Following someone on a social network or "module A imports module B" are directed relationships.
example: A one-way street system is a directed graph: A→B does not imply B→A.

definition: The number of edge ends touching a vertex: how many neighbours it has in a simple undirected graph. A graph self-loop adds 2. Adding up all degrees gives twice the number of edges.
example: In a triangle every vertex has degree 2, and 2 + 2 + 2 = 6 = 2 × 3 edges.

definition: In a directed graph, the number of edges arriving at a vertex (arrows pointing in). Kahn's topological sort repeatedly removes vertices whose in-degree has fallen to 0.
example: If A→C and B→C are the only edges into C, C has in-degree 2.

definition: In a directed graph, the number of edges leaving a vertex (arrows pointing out). The out-degrees of all vertices add up to the number of edges.
example: A web page with 12 outgoing links has out-degree 12.

definition: The fact that in any undirected graph the vertex degrees add up to exactly twice the number of edges, because every edge has two ends. A consequence is that the number of odd-degree vertices is always even.
example: Degrees 3, 3, 2, 2, 2 add up to 12, so the graph has 6 edges.

definition: A sequence of vertices in which each consecutive pair is joined by an edge; unlike a simple path, it may repeat vertices and edges. A closed walk ends where it started.
example: A→B→A→C is a walk of 3 edges that revisits A.

definition: A walk that never visits the same vertex twice. A shortest path in a graph without negative cycles can always be taken to be simple, so it has at most n − 1 edges for n vertices.
example: A→B→C is a simple path; A→B→A→C is not.

definition: A path in a directed graph that follows the arrows and returns to its start. A directed graph has a topological order exactly when it has no directed cycle.
example: A→B, B→C and C→A form a directed cycle, so there is no valid build order for A, B and C.

definition: A graph with relatively few edges: the edge count m is closer to the vertex count n than to the maximum possible, about n²/2. Road networks and many other real-world graphs are sparse, which is why adjacency lists are the usual representation.
example: A 1000 × 1000 grid has about 10⁶ vertices but only about 2 × 10⁶ edges.

definition: A graph with no graph self-loops and at most one edge between any pair of vertices (one in each direction, if directed). Many textbook bounds, such as at most n(n − 1)/2 edges, assume a simple graph.
example: A social network where each friendship is recorded once is a simple graph.

definition: A graph that may have several edges joining the same pair of vertices (parallel edges). Algorithms that ignore "the edge back to my parent" must then distinguish edges by id, because a doubled link is not a bridge.
example: Two separate cables between the same pair of routers are parallel edges.

definition: An edge that starts and ends at the same vertex, u→u. It adds 2 to an undirected vertex's degree, simple graphs forbid it, and in shortest-path tables a negative one makes that vertex's distance to itself negative.
example: A directed graph on 5 vertices could have up to 25 edges if graph self-loops were allowed, but only 20 without them.

definition: A vertex with no edges at all (degree 0). It is still a connected component of size 1, and it never appears in an adjacency dictionary built only from an edge list.
example: A new user with no friends is an isolated vertex in a friendship graph.

definition: A graph representation that stores, for each vertex, a list of its neighbours (and edge weights if any). It uses space proportional to n + m and lists a vertex's neighbours in time proportional to its degree, so it is the default for BFS, DFS and Dijkstra.
example: adj = {0: [1, 2], 1: [0, 2]} says vertex 0 is joined to 1 and 2.

definition: A graph representation as an n × n table where entry [u][v] is 1 (or the edge weight) if there is an edge u→v. Edge lookup is constant time, but it always uses n² cells and listing a vertex's neighbours costs n.
example: A million-vertex graph needs 10¹² cells, about 125 GB even at one bit per cell.

definition: A graph representation that is simply a list of (u, v) or (u, v, weight) tuples. It suits algorithms that process every edge, such as Kruskal's (which sorts them) and Bellman–Ford, and is how graphs often arrive from files.
example: edges = [(0, 1, 4), (0, 2, 1)] describes two weighted edges.

definition: A compact graph or sparse-matrix layout that stores all neighbour lists back to back in one flat array, plus an offsets array saying where each vertex's neighbours start. It is memory-efficient and cache-friendly.
example: With 32-bit integers, a million vertices and 10 million directed edges need about 44 MB.

definition: A graph that is never stored: a rule or function generates a vertex's neighbours when asked. Grids, puzzle states and game positions are usually searched as implicit graphs.
example: A lock with 4 dials of 10 digits is an implicit graph of 10,000 dial settings, each with 8 neighbours.

definition: The set of all configurations (states) a problem can be in, viewed as the vertices of a graph whose edges are the legal moves. Searching it with BFS finds the fewest moves.
example: In the 15-puzzle each board arrangement is a state; there are about 10¹³ reachable ones.

definition: A sliding puzzle with 15 numbered tiles and one gap on a 4 × 4 board; you slide tiles into the gap to sort them. Its roughly 10¹³ reachable states make it a classic example of a huge implicit graph.
example: Each legal slide is one edge between two board states.

definition: A puzzle that turns one word into another by changing one letter at a time, each step being a real word. Modelled as a graph of words linked when they differ by one letter, BFS finds the shortest ladder.
example: COLD → CORD → CARD → WARD → WARM.

definition: A speed-up technique for road-network shortest paths: preprocessing ranks vertices by importance and adds shortcut edges, so each later query explores only a tiny part of the graph.
example: Routing engines preprocess a country's road graph once, then answer millions of queries quickly.

definition: The set (or array of flags) a traversal uses to remember which vertices it has already discovered, so it never processes one twice and cannot loop forever on a cycle.
example: BFS stores dist[v] when it first enqueues v; that dictionary doubles as the visited set.

definition: The vertices a search has discovered but not yet expanded: BFS's queue or DFS's stack. Its size is the main memory cost of searching huge trees.
example: In a tree with 10 children per node, BFS at depth 6 holds about a million frontier nodes; DFS holds about 60.

definition: The number of children each node has in a search tree (or the average number of neighbours). A search to depth d in a tree with branching factor b touches roughly b to the power d nodes.
example: Chess has an average branching factor of roughly 30 to 35 legal moves.

definition: A search that runs depth-limited DFS with limits 0, 1, 2, … until it finds the goal. It finds a shallowest goal like BFS but uses only DFS's small memory; repeating the shallow levels costs only about b/(b − 1) times as many visits for branching factor b.
example: With branching factor 10 and depth 6, it makes about 11% more visits than BFS.

definition: Finding all cells connected to a starting cell in a grid, as the paint-bucket tool does, or counting separate regions such as islands. It is BFS or DFS over the grid's implicit graph.
example: Counting islands in a map of land and water is one flood fill per unvisited land cell.

definition: BFS started with several sources in the queue at distance 0, giving every vertex its distance to the nearest source in a single O(n + m) pass.
example: Distance from every cell of a building to its nearest exit, computed in one search.

definition: Searching from the start and the goal at the same time until the two frontiers meet. Each side only goes about half the depth, which in a tree-like graph shrinks the work from roughly b^d to about 2 × b^(d/2).
example: With 100 contacts each and 6 hops, two half-searches touch about 2 million people instead of a trillion.

definition: A garbage-collection method that first marks every object reachable from the program's roots by traversing the reference graph, then sweeps (frees) every unmarked object.
example: An object no longer referenced from any variable is not marked and gets freed.

definition: A maximal group of vertices in an undirected graph where every vertex can reach every other. Counting components means starting a new traversal from each still-unvisited vertex.
example: Edges 0–1, 1–2, 3–4 on vertices 0–5 give components {0, 1, 2}, {3, 4} and {5}.

definition: Whether a path exists from one vertex to another. Any complete BFS or DFS from a vertex finds exactly the vertices reachable from it.
example: In a one-way road network, B may be reachable from A but not A from B.

definition: A DFS bookkeeping scheme: white means not yet discovered, grey means discovered and still on the recursion stack, black means finished. An edge to a grey vertex is a back edge, which proves a directed cycle.
example: Meeting an already-black vertex is not a cycle: it is a cross or forward edge.

definition: In a DFS, an edge from a vertex to one of its own ancestors still on the stack (a grey vertex). A directed graph has a cycle exactly when DFS finds a back edge.
example: With DFS path 0→1→2, an edge 2→0 is a back edge closing the cycle 0→1→2→0.

definition: In a DFS (or BFS), an edge the search followed to discover a new vertex. The tree edges together form the search tree or forest.
example: If DFS goes from 0 to undiscovered 1, the edge 0→1 is a tree edge.

definition: In a directed DFS, an edge to an already-finished (black) vertex: a forward edge if that vertex is a descendant, a cross edge otherwise. Neither closes a cycle.
example: In the diamond 0→1→3, 0→2→3, the edge 2→3 is a cross edge.

definition: An ordering of a directed graph's vertices so that every edge u→v has u before v. It exists exactly when the graph has no directed cycle, and there are often many valid orders.
example: Socks before shoes and shirt before tie: one valid order is socks, shirt, tie, shoes.

definition: A topological sort that repeatedly outputs a vertex with in-degree 0 and deletes its outgoing edges, using a queue. If it outputs fewer than n vertices, the graph has a cycle. It runs in O(n + m).
example: For edges A→C, B→C it starts with A and B, then C.

definition: The order in which DFS finishes vertices, that is, returns from them after exploring everything reachable. Reversing it gives a topological order of a DAG; Kosaraju's algorithm also relies on it.
example: For A→C→E, DFS finishes E, then C, then A; reversed: A, C, E.

definition: A maximal set of vertices in a directed graph where each can reach every other. Every vertex belongs to exactly one SCC, possibly on its own.
example: Edges 0→1, 1→2, 2→0 make {0, 1, 2} one SCC.

definition: The graph you get by collapsing each strongly connected component to a single vertex and keeping edges between different components. It is always a DAG, so it can be topologically sorted.
example: Three SCCs linked A→B←C condense to a three-vertex DAG.

definition: An SCC algorithm with two DFS passes: one on the graph to record finish order, then one on the reversed graph taking vertices in decreasing finish time. Each tree of the second pass is one SCC. O(n + m).
example: It needs the transpose (reversed) graph, unlike Tarjan's.

definition: A one-pass DFS algorithm for strongly connected components that tracks discovery indices and low-link values on a stack, emitting each SCC (sinks first, in reverse topological order) when its root finishes. O(n + m).
example: It finds SCCs without building the reversed graph.

definition: In a DFS, the smallest discovery time reachable from a vertex's subtree using tree edges plus at most one extra (back) edge. It powers Tarjan's SCC algorithm and the bridge and articulation-point tests.
example: If low[v] > tin[u] for tree edge u–v, nothing in v's subtree can get back to u or above, so u–v is a bridge.

definition: The counter value at which DFS first reaches a vertex: 0 for the first, 1 for the next and so on. Written tin[u] or idx[u] in the code.
example: DFS from 0 visiting 0, 1, 2 gives tin values 0, 1, 2.

definition: The same directed graph with every edge reversed. It has the same strongly connected components as the original, which Kosaraju's algorithm exploits.
example: The transpose of A→B is B→A.

definition: The problem of deciding whether a formula made of clauses with two true/false literals each can be satisfied. It is solved in linear time by building an implication graph and checking that no variable shares an SCC with its negation.
example: (x or y) and (not x or y) is satisfiable with y true.

definition: A directed graph with a vertex for each variable and its negation, and an edge a→b for each implication "if a then b". It is how 2-SAT is turned into an SCC problem.
example: The clause (x or y) gives edges not x → y and not y → x.

definition: A graph whose vertices split into two sides so that every edge joins the two sides, such as workers and jobs. A graph is bipartite exactly when it has no odd-length cycle, which BFS 2-colouring checks in O(n + m).
example: A square (4-cycle) is bipartite; a triangle is not.

definition: A cycle with an odd number of edges. Alternating two colours around it must clash, so any graph containing one is not bipartite.
example: A triangle and a pentagon are odd cycles.

definition: A Python standard-library module (since 3.9) whose TopologicalSorter class orders a dependency graph and can hand out, via get_ready(), every task whose prerequisites are done, ready to run in parallel.
example: ts = TopologicalSorter({"b": {"a"}}); list(ts.static_order()) gives ["a", "b"].

definition: A classic build tool that reads rules saying which files depend on which, and rebuilds only out-of-date targets in dependency order.
example: If main.o depends on main.c, Make recompiles main.o only when main.c is newer.

definition: An open-source build and test tool from Google that models a codebase as a graph of targets and dependencies, building them in dependency order and caching results.
example: A monorepo with thousands of targets can rebuild only what a change affects.

definition: A build tool widely used for Java and Android projects that runs tasks as a directed acyclic graph of dependencies.
example: The compileJava task runs before test because test depends on it.

definition: A single version-control repository that holds the code for many projects or services, often built with dependency-graph tools such as Bazel.
example: One repository containing 50,000 build targets for every team.

definition: The basic shortest-path step: for an edge u→v of weight w, if dist(u) + w is less than dist(v), lower dist(v) to that value and record u as v's parent. Dijkstra, Bellman–Ford and A* differ only in which edges they relax and when.
example: If dist(u) = 3, w = 4 and dist(v) = 9, relaxing sets dist(v) to 7.

definition: The problem of finding the cheapest distance from one source vertex to every other vertex. Dijkstra, Bellman–Ford, 0-1 BFS and BFS all solve versions of it.
example: Distances from one warehouse to every delivery address.

definition: A shortest-path algorithm's current best guess at a vertex's distance, starting at infinity and only ever decreasing as better routes are found. It becomes final when the algorithm settles the vertex.
example: In Dijkstra, C's tentative distance can drop from 9 to 6 before C is popped.

definition: In Dijkstra's algorithm, a vertex whose shortest distance is final because it was popped with the smallest tentative distance. With non-negative weights no later path can beat it.
example: Popping B with distance 1 settles B.

definition: An outdated item left in a priority queue after a cheaper entry for the same vertex was pushed. Lazy-deletion Dijkstra simply skips it when it is popped.
example: After pushing (3, A), the earlier (4, A) entry is stale.

definition: A cycle whose edge weights add up to less than zero. Going round it repeatedly makes paths ever cheaper, so vertices reachable from it have no shortest distance (it is minus infinity). Bellman–Ford detects one reachable from its source.
example: Edges A→B 1, B→C −3, C→A 1 total −1: a negative cycle.

definition: An edge whose weight is below zero, such as a rebate. Dijkstra's correctness proof fails with them; Bellman–Ford, DAG relaxation and Floyd–Warshall handle them if there is no negative cycle.
example: A −3 edge can make a three-edge route cheaper than a direct one.

definition: A single-source shortest-path algorithm that relaxes every edge n − 1 times, which handles negative edges in O(nm) time. If an n-th round still improves a distance, a negative cycle is reachable from the source.
example: On 10⁵ vertices and 10⁶ edges, its worst case is about 10¹¹ relaxations.

definition: A queue-based variant of Bellman–Ford that only re-relaxes edges leaving vertices whose distance just changed. It is often fast in practice, but its worst case is still O(nm).
example: A vertex is re-queued only after its distance improves.

definition: A distance-vector routing protocol in which each router repeatedly shares its distance table with its neighbours, in effect running a distributed Bellman–Ford. It limits routes to 15 hops.
example: A router learns "network X is 3 hops away via router B" from B's advertisement.

definition: A family of routing protocols in which each router tells its neighbours its current distance to every destination, and each router keeps the best route it hears of: a distributed Bellman–Ford.
example: RIP is the classic distance-vector protocol.

definition: Making a risk-free profit from price differences, for example a cycle of currency exchanges that ends with more money than it started. Weighting each exchange by minus the logarithm of its rate turns such a cycle into a negative cycle.
example: USD→EUR 0.9, EUR→GBP 0.9, GBP→USD 1.25 multiply to 1.0125: a 1.25% gain before fees.

definition: A shortest-path method for graphs whose weights are only 0 or 1: a deque replaces Dijkstra's heap, with 0-weight moves pushed to the front and 1-weight moves to the back. It runs in O(n + m).
example: Fewest walls to break in a maze: stepping into a wall costs 1, open floor 0.

definition: A shortest-path search towards one goal that orders its heap by f = g + h: the known cost so far plus a heuristic estimate of the remaining cost. With an admissible heuristic (and the usual reopening rules) it returns an optimal path while usually exploring fewer vertices than Dijkstra.
example: Pathfinding in games uses A* with Manhattan or octile distance on a grid.

definition: An A* heuristic that never overestimates the true remaining cost to the goal. Under the standard conditions it guarantees A* returns an optimal path.
example: On a 4-way grid with cost-1 moves, Manhattan distance is admissible; twice Manhattan is not.

definition: An A* heuristic h with h(u) ≤ w(u, v) + h(v) for every edge u→v: it never drops by more than the cost of the step. With h(goal) = 0 it is also admissible, and A* never needs to reopen a settled vertex.
example: Straight-line distance on a road map is consistent when every road is at least as long as the straight line.

definition: The distance between two grid cells counted as the absolute difference in rows plus the absolute difference in columns, as if moving only along streets. It is the standard admissible heuristic on a 4-way grid.
The ordinary straight-line distance between two points: the square root of the sum of the squared coordinate differences. It never exceeds the Manhattan distance.
example: From (0, 0) to (3, 4) it is 5.

definition: The larger of the row difference and the column difference between two cells. It is the exact move count on an 8-way grid where diagonal moves also cost 1, like a chess king.
example: From (0, 0) to (3, 5) it is 5.

definition: A grid heuristic for 8-way movement where straight moves cost 1 and diagonals cost √2 (about 1.41): take as many diagonal steps as the smaller coordinate difference, then straight steps for the rest.
example: For differences 3 and 5: 3 × 1.41 + 2 ≈ 6.24.

definition: A* with the heuristic multiplied by a weight λ greater than 1, which searches more greedily towards the goal. Under the standard conditions with an admissible heuristic, the path it returns costs at most λ times the optimum.
example: With λ = 1.5 and an optimal cost of 100, the returned path costs at most 150.

definition: A route-planning technique that precomputes distances to a few landmark vertices and uses the triangle inequality to derive strong admissible A* heuristics.
example: Knowing the distances to a landmark on the coast bounds how far any two inland towns are apart.

definition: The rule that going directly is never longer than going via a third point: d(a, c) ≤ d(a, b) + d(b, c). Shortest-path distances, Euclidean distance and metric TSP all satisfy it.
example: If A is 3 from B and B is 4 from C, A is at most 7 from C.

definition: The tree formed by each vertex's parent pointer after a single-source shortest-path run: following parents from any vertex back to the source gives a shortest path. It is generally different from a minimum spanning tree.
example: In a triangle S–A 2, S–B 2, A–B 1, the shortest-path tree from S uses S–A and S–B.

definition: Finding shortest paths in a directed acyclic graph by relaxing each vertex's outgoing edges in topological order. Each vertex is final when reached, even with negative weights, and the whole run is O(n + m).
example: Critical-path scheduling of tasks uses the same idea.

definition: The problem of finding the shortest distance between every ordered pair of vertices, producing an n × n table. Floyd–Warshall, n runs of Dijkstra and Johnson's algorithm solve it.
example: 300 depots need a 300 × 300 table of 90,000 distances.

definition: The largest shortest-path distance between any two vertices of a connected graph: how far apart the two most distant vertices are.
example: A path of 5 vertices has diameter 4.

definition: An all-pairs shortest-path algorithm that, for each vertex k in turn, checks whether going through k shortens the route between every pair i, j. It is three nested loops, O(n³) time and O(n²) space, and handles negative edges; a negative diagonal entry reveals a negative cycle.
example: With n = 500 it makes 1.25 × 10⁸ inner-loop iterations.

definition: A vertex a path passes through strictly between its start and end. Floyd–Warshall's DP gradually allows more intermediate vertices.
example: In 1→2→3→0, the intermediate vertices are 2 and 3.

definition: A table storing, for each pair (i, j), the first vertex to move to on a shortest path from i to j. Following it hop by hop reconstructs the whole path.
example: If nxt[0][4] = 2, nxt[2][4] = 1 and nxt[1][4] = 4, the path is 0, 2, 1, 4.

definition: For a directed graph, the relation "j is reachable from i" for every pair, often stored as a Boolean matrix. Warshall's algorithm computes it by replacing min and + in Floyd–Warshall with OR and AND.
example: If A depends on B and B on C, the closure records that A depends on C.

definition: The Boolean version of Floyd–Warshall that computes transitive closure: i reaches j if it already did, or if i reaches k and k reaches j. O(n³), or less with bitsets.
example: Packing rows into 64-bit words divides the work by about 64.

definition: A fixed-size sequence of bits packed into machine words, so one CPU instruction can operate on 64 true/false values at once (with 64-bit words). Used to speed up transitive closure and set operations.
example: A row of 10,000 reachability flags fits in 157 64-bit words.

definition: The number of bits a CPU handles in one ordinary operation, typically 64 on modern processors. Bitset algorithms divide their work by it.
example: An OR of two 64-bit words combines 64 bit pairs at once.

definition: The algebra of true/false values with OR playing the role of addition and AND of multiplication. Substituting it for (min, +) turns Floyd–Warshall into transitive closure.
example: true OR false = true; true AND false = false.

definition: An all-pairs shortest-path method for sparse graphs with negative edges: one Bellman–Ford run computes vertex potentials, every edge is reweighted to be non-negative, then Dijkstra runs from every vertex. With binary heaps it is O(n(n + m) log n).
example: An edge u→v of weight −3 with h(u) = 0 and h(v) = −3 gets new weight 0.

definition: A number h(v) attached to each vertex, used to reweight edges as w(u, v) + h(u) − h(v). Along any path the potentials cancel in pairs, so every path between the same endpoints shifts equally and shortest paths are preserved.
example: Johnson's algorithm takes h(v) as v's distance from an extra source.

definition: A special value standing for "no path", such as float('inf') in Python or a large integer like INT_MAX in C. With fixed-size integers, adding two such values can overflow, so code must skip additions involving it.
example: INT_MAX + INT_MAX overflows in C, which is undefined behaviour for signed int.

definition: A widely used Python library for creating and analysing graphs, with ready-made shortest-path, flow, matching and centrality algorithms.
example: networkx.floyd_warshall(G) returns all-pairs distances.

definition: A subset of a connected undirected graph's edges that connects every vertex without forming a cycle. It always has exactly n − 1 edges for n vertices.
example: A 6-vertex graph's spanning trees each have 5 edges.

definition: A spanning tree whose edge weights add up to the least possible total. Kruskal's and Prim's greedy algorithms find one; it is unique when all weights are distinct. On a disconnected graph the analogue is a minimum spanning forest.
example: Connecting 6 offices with fibre at the lowest total cost.

definition: A split of a graph's vertices into two non-empty groups. An edge crosses the cut if its ends are on different sides. Cuts underpin the MST cut property and the max-flow min-cut theorem.
example: Splitting {A, C} from the rest, the crossing edges are those with exactly one end in {A, C}.

definition: For any cut of a graph, the lightest edge crossing it belongs to some minimum spanning tree (to every MST if it is strictly lightest). It is why Kruskal's and Prim's greedy choices are safe.
example: If B–C (3) is the lightest edge leaving {A, B}, every MST contains it when weights are distinct.

definition: For any cycle, an edge strictly heavier than every other edge on that cycle belongs to no minimum spanning tree.
example: If a new cheap edge closes a cycle whose heaviest edge weighs 5, that 5-weight edge can be dropped.

definition: An MST algorithm that sorts all edges by weight and adds each one unless it would join two vertices already connected, a test answered by Union-Find. O(m log m) time, dominated by the sort.
example: Stopping early with k components gives single-linkage clustering.

definition: An MST algorithm that grows one tree from a start vertex, each step adding the lightest edge leaving the tree. It looks like Dijkstra but orders the heap by single edge weight. O(m log n) with a heap, O(n²) with an array.
example: The array version suits complete graphs such as all pairs of points in the plane.

definition: An MST algorithm, published by Otakar Borůvka in 1926 for planning an electricity network in Moravia, in which every component simultaneously picks its cheapest outgoing edge each round. The component count at least halves per round, and the rounds parallelise well.
example: A 1,000-vertex graph needs at most 10 rounds.

definition: Another name for the Union-Find data structure: it keeps elements in non-overlapping sets, each a tree of parent pointers whose root is the set's representative, with find and union operations.
example: Kruskal's cycle test is one find on each endpoint.

definition: The two Union-Find operations: find(x) follows parent pointers to return the root (representative) of x's set; union(a, b) merges the sets containing a and b by linking one root under the other.
example: If find(u) equals find(v), u and v are already connected.

definition: The element at the root of a Union-Find tree, which identifies its whole set: two elements are in the same set exactly when find returns the same representative.
example: After union(0, 1), both find(0) and find(1) return 0.

definition: A Union-Find rule: attach the root with the lower rank (an upper bound on tree height) under the one with the higher rank. A tree of rank r has at least 2 to the power r nodes, so heights stay at most log₂ n.
example: With a million elements no tree is taller than about 20.

definition: A Union-Find optimisation: during find, point every node on the path straight at the root, so later finds take one step. Combined with union by rank it gives inverse-Ackermann amortised cost.
example: After find(2) on the chain 2 → 1 → 0, both 1 and 2 point directly at 0.

definition: An extraordinarily slowly growing function, written α(n), that bounds the amortised cost of Union-Find with union by rank and path compression. It is at most about 4 for any input size that could fit in a real computer.
example: 10⁷ operations on 10⁶ elements cost O(10⁷ α(10⁶)): effectively linear.

definition: A clustering method that repeatedly merges the two closest clusters, where cluster distance is the closest pair between them. Running Kruskal and stopping at k components produces it and maximises the spacing, the smallest distance between different clusters.
example: Stopping Kruskal at 3 components on the lesson graph gives spacing 3.

definition: Finding the shortest tour that visits every city exactly once and returns home. It is NP-hard; for metric TSP (distances obey the triangle inequality), doubling an MST and shortcutting gives a tour at most twice optimal.
example: If the MST weighs 100 km, the doubled-MST tour is at most 200 km.

definition: The directed analogue of a spanning tree: a set of edges giving exactly one directed path from a chosen root to every vertex. A minimum-weight one is found by the Chu–Liu/Edmonds algorithm, not by Kruskal or Prim.
example: Broadcasting from one server to all others along one-way links.

definition: An algorithm for the minimum spanning arborescence of a directed graph: each vertex picks its cheapest incoming edge, and any resulting cycles are contracted and resolved recursively.
example: It is the directed counterpart of an MST algorithm.

definition: A way of joining a set of points in the plane into triangles so that no point lies inside any triangle's circumscribed circle. For distinct points it contains a Euclidean MST and has only O(n) edges.
example: An MST of 10,000 points can be found from about 30,000 Delaunay edges instead of 5 × 10⁷ pairs.

definition: The elements in exactly one of two sets. Comparing two spanning trees, it is the edges belonging to one tree but not the other.
example: The symmetric difference of {1, 2, 3} and {2, 3, 4} is {1, 4}.

definition: The number of independent cycles in a graph: m − n + c for m edges, n vertices and c connected components. A connected graph with one more edge than a tree has exactly one cycle.
example: 6 routers joined by 6 cables in one network have 6 − 6 + 1 = 1 cycle.

definition: An Ethernet network protocol that blocks redundant switch links so the active topology is a tree, preventing frames from looping endlessly and causing broadcast storms.
example: A ring of switches has one link blocked by STP until another link fails.

definition: A directed graph where each edge has an edge capacity, with a source s where flow starts and a sink t where it ends. A flow sends amounts along edges without exceeding capacities and without creating or losing flow at intermediate vertices.
example: Pipes with capacities in litres per second from a reservoir to a city.

definition: The maximum amount an edge of a flow network can carry, such as litres per second, Gbit/s or lorries per day. Flow on an edge must stay between 0 and its edge capacity.
example: A link with an edge capacity of 10 Gbit/s cannot carry 12 Gbit/s.

definition: The two special vertices of a flow network: the source s, where all flow starts, and the sink t, where it ends. Every other vertex must pass on exactly what it receives.
example: In a matching reduction, the source feeds every worker and every job feeds the sink.

definition: The rule that at every vertex except the source and sink, the total flow in equals the total flow out.
example: A junction receiving 7 units must send out 7.

definition: The largest total amount that can be sent from source to sink in a flow network without exceeding any edge capacity. With integer capacities there is always an integer maximum flow.
example: In the lesson's example network the maximum flow is 14.

definition: The graph of what you could still do to a flow: each edge u→v has forward residual capacity (edge capacity minus flow) and a backward residual v→u equal to its flow, which lets later paths cancel earlier choices.
example: An edge with edge capacity 10 carrying 6 has forward residual 4 and backward residual 6.

definition: A source-to-sink path in the residual graph with unused edge capacity on every edge. Pushing its bottleneck amount along it increases the flow; when none exists, the flow is maximum.
example: After a bad first path, s→b→a→t uses a backward edge to reroute flow.

definition: The smallest unused edge capacity along a path, which is the most the path can carry.
example: A path with unused edge capacities 7 and 4 has bottleneck 4.

definition: The general max-flow method: while an augmenting path exists in the residual graph, push its bottleneck capacity along it. With integer capacities it terminates after at most as many augmentations as the flow value; path choice matters.
example: A badly chosen path sequence can need 2,000,000 augmentations where 2 suffice.

definition: Ford–Fulkerson with each augmenting path chosen by BFS as a shortest (fewest-edge) path. That bounds the number of augmentations independently of capacities, giving O(n m²) time.
example: On the classic bad case it needs just 2 augmentations.

definition: A faster max-flow algorithm that builds BFS distance levels and pushes a blocking flow along many shortest paths at once. O(n²m) in general and O(m√n) on unit networks such as the bipartite-matching reduction (n vertices, m edges).
example: It is a common choice for max flow in programming contests.

definition: In Dinic's algorithm, a flow in the level graph that saturates at least one edge on every shortest source-to-sink path, so no more shortest paths remain.
example: Each Dinic phase finds one blocking flow, then rebuilds the levels.

definition: A family of max-flow algorithms that let vertices hold excess flow temporarily and push it towards the sink using height labels, instead of finding whole augmenting paths.
example: Many high-performance max-flow solvers are push–relabel variants.

definition: The fact that if every edge capacity is an integer, some maximum flow uses only integer amounts on every edge, and augmenting-path algorithms find one. It is what lets flow solve assignment and counting problems.
example: With unit capacities, each worker sends either 0 or 1 unit, never 0.5.

definition: A split of a flow network's vertices into S, containing the source, and T, containing the sink. Its cut capacity is the total edge capacity of edges from S to T; a minimum cut has the smallest such total.
example: Cutting {s, a, b, c} from {t} in the lesson example gives cut capacity 4 + 10 = 14.

definition: The theorem that the maximum flow from s to t equals the minimum cut capacity over all s–t cuts. The vertices still reachable from s in the final residual graph give such a minimum cut.
example: Flow 14 and a cut whose cut capacity is 14 prove each other optimal.

definition: An edge in a flow network whose flow equals its edge capacity, so it has no forward residual capacity left.
example: Every edge from S to T in a minimum cut is saturated at maximum flow.

definition: The theorem that the maximum number of edge-disjoint paths between two vertices equals the minimum number of edges whose removal disconnects them. It is max-flow min-cut with unit capacities.
example: If 3 links must fail to separate two data centres, there are 3 link-disjoint routes between them.

definition: Paths between the same two vertices that share no edge. Their maximum number equals the max flow with unit capacities.
example: Two routes between data centres that use no common cable are edge-disjoint.

definition: Dividing an image into regions, such as foreground and background. The "graph cuts" method models pixels as vertices and finds a minimum s–t cut that balances pixel preferences against cutting between similar neighbours.
example: Separating a person from the background of a photo.

definition: The problem of deciding whether a sports team can still finish top given the remaining fixtures. It reduces to a maximum-flow computation.
example: A team is eliminated if even winning every remaining game cannot let it overtake the leaders.

definition: Choosing a profitable set of projects when some projects require others; it reduces to a minimum cut in a suitably built flow network.
example: Pick projects to maximise profit minus the cost of the equipment they need.

definition: A flow network in which every vertex other than the source and sink has either exactly one incoming edge or exactly one outgoing edge, and that single edge has an edge capacity of 1, as in the standard bipartite-matching reduction. Dinic's algorithm runs in O(m√n) on such networks (n vertices, m edges).
example: Source → workers → jobs → sink with all capacities 1 is a unit network.

definition: A set of edges in which no two share a vertex, so each vertex is paired with at most one other. In bipartite graphs it models assignments such as riders to drivers.
example: Ann–X, Bob–Y and Cat–Z form a matching of size 3.

definition: A matching with as many edges as possible. In a bipartite graph it equals an integer maximum flow in the network source → left side → right side → sink with all capacities 1.
example: Pairing as many interns with acceptable projects as possible.

definition: A simple bipartite-matching algorithm: for each left vertex, a DFS looks for a free right vertex or one whose partner can be moved elsewhere (an augmenting path). O(n m) in the worst case.
example: Bob wants X, so Ann is asked to move from X to Y.

definition: A bipartite-matching algorithm that finds a maximal set of shortest augmenting paths in each phase, needing only O(√n) phases, for O((n + m)√n) time overall.
example: For 10⁵ riders, 10⁵ drivers and 10⁶ compatible pairs, its conventional O(m√n) bound is about 4.5 × 10⁸, versus about 10¹¹ for Kuhn's algorithm.

definition: Pairing agents with tasks one-to-one so the total cost is as small as possible (or total profit as large). It is solved by the Hungarian algorithm or min-cost flow.
example: Assign drivers to riders to minimise the total pickup time.

definition: A flow problem where each edge also has a cost per unit of flow, and the goal is to send a required amount from source to sink as cheaply as possible. It generalises shortest paths, max flow and assignment.
example: Shipping goods through a network with per-tonne transport costs.

definition: The theorem that in a bipartite graph the size of a maximum matching equals the size of a minimum vertex cover. It makes minimum vertex cover easy in bipartite graphs, although it is NP-hard in general.
example: If the maximum matching has 7 edges, 7 guards suffice to watch every corridor.

definition: A set of vertices that touches every edge of a graph. Finding a smallest one is NP-hard in general, but easy in bipartite graphs by König's theorem.
example: Choosing rooms for guards so every corridor has a guard at one end.

definition: An edge of an undirected graph whose removal increases the number of connected components: it lies on no cycle. In a network it is a single link whose failure splits the network.
example: A router with only one cable to the rest of the network hangs off a bridge.

definition: A vertex of an undirected graph whose removal, with its edges, increases the number of connected components: a single point of failure. DFS low-link values find all of them in O(n + m).
example: A router everything passes through to reach one branch office.

definition: A maximal part of an undirected graph that stays connected after removing any single edge. Deleting all bridges splits a graph into these components.
example: Two triangles joined by one link form two 2-edge-connected components.

definition: A maximal group of edges in which any two edges lie on a common simple cycle, so no single vertex removal disconnects it. Articulation points are where these components meet.
example: Each triangle in the lesson example is its own biconnected component.

definition: A component whose failure alone takes down a system or cuts part of it off. In a network graph, bridges and articulation points are single points of failure.
example: One fibre link between two regions.

definition: Deciding whether a graph can be drawn in the plane with no crossing edges. Linear-time algorithms first split the graph into biconnected components.
example: A circuit layout tool checks planarity before routing wires on one layer.

definition: A vertex with exactly one edge (degree 1), hanging off the rest of the graph. Its single edge is always a bridge.
example: R7 connected only to R4 is a pendant vertex.

definition: The class of decision problems whose "yes" answers can be checked quickly (in polynomial time) given a suitable certificate. Whether every such problem can also be solved quickly is the open P versus NP question.
example: Checking a proposed TSP tour against a length limit is quick even though finding the best tour seems hard.

definition: The open question of whether every problem whose solutions can be checked quickly can also be solved quickly. Most researchers believe not, which is why NP-hard problems such as TSP are assumed to have no polynomial-time algorithm.
example: A fast exact TSP algorithm would prove P = NP.

definition: Growth by a constant factor per step, like b to the power d in a search tree. Exponential searches become infeasible quickly as depth grows.
example: With 10 choices per step, depth 6 gives a million nodes and depth 12 a trillion.

definition: A network failure where broadcast frames circulate endlessly around a loop of switches, multiplying until they saturate the links. Spanning Tree Protocol exists to prevent it.
example: Plugging both ends of a cable into the same switch network can trigger a storm without STP.

definition: A directed graph in which an edge records that one item depends on another, such as a package requiring a library or a build target requiring a file. Build order is a topological order of it, and circular dependencies are cycles.
example: app → lib1 → core says app needs lib1, which needs core.

definition: The predicted time until a vehicle or delivery arrives. Ride-hailing dispatch uses driver ETAs as the costs in a weighted assignment.
example: A driver 4 minutes away has an ETA of 4 minutes.

definition: A 3 × 3 × 3 twisting puzzle whose roughly 4.3 × 10¹⁹ positions form a famous state-space graph, with one edge per legal twist.
example: Every position can be solved in at most 20 face turns.

definition: A data rate of one billion (10⁹) bits per second, used for network link capacities.
example: A 10 Gbit/s link moves at most about 1.25 GB of data per second.

definition: One CPU instruction acting on a whole machine word, such as an OR of two 64-bit words. Bitset algorithms count their cost in word operations.
example: ORing two 10,000-bit rows takes 157 word operations with 64-bit words.

definition: Shorthand used in mathematics for "if and only if": each statement implies the other, so they are either both true or both false.
example: A directed graph has a topological order iff it has no directed cycle.

definition: The two basic true/false operations: OR is true if either input is true, AND only if both are. Transitive closure replaces Floyd–Warshall's min with OR and + with AND.
example: true OR false is true; true AND false is false.

definition: Short for dynamic programming: solving a problem by combining stored answers to smaller overlapping subproblems. Floyd–Warshall is a DP over which intermediate vertices are allowed.
example: d_k[i][j] is built from the table for k − 1.

definition: The ISO 4217 codes for the US dollar, the euro and the pound sterling, used when quoting exchange rates.
example: A USD→EUR rate of 0.9 means one dollar buys 0.9 euros.

definition: An algorithm for a hard optimisation problem that runs quickly and guarantees its answer is within a known factor of the best. The doubled-MST tour is a 2-approximation for metric TSP.
example: A tour at most twice the optimum length.
